To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The duration of wars is shorter if a foreign affairs minister who is blamed for poor war performance is replaced by the leader.

(1) the replacement of the foreign affairs minister is a common practice in the aftermath of war, (2) the foreign affairs minister has the greatest influence on the war duration, (3) the replacement of foreign affairs minister reduces the duration of war, and (4) the replacement of a foreign affairs minister reduces war duration more in wars that end with a defeat than in those that end with a victory.

the duration of wars that end in a defeat for the decider is shorter when he replaces his minister of foreign affairs, especially when the war is costly and the minister is a scapegoat, but only when the war is initiated by the decider himself.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we show that scapegoating is an important mechanism to reduce the duration of wars that end in military defeat, and that this mechanism is particularly important in the context of foreign policy failures.
the duration of interstate war is shorter when leaders are held accountable for poor war results.

we show that leaders can avoid domestic punishment for poor outcomes of war by replacing cabinet ministers for foreign affairs, and that these ministers are more likely to be replaced when wars end in defeat.
The main takeaway from our work is that
leaders do not need to continue fighting a losing war to avoid punishment.
leaders who are responsible for war outcomes can avoid punishment by scapegoating their cabinet ministers.
the replacement of cabinet members responsible for foreign policy decisions can reduce the duration of wars that end in failure.
